Issued at 122 PM CDT Fri Sep 4 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: It remains hot and very humid across the Tri-State 
area, as temperatures have already risen into the upper 80s to low 
90s.  The generally weak surface flow has allowed dew points to 
remain in the upper 60s to lower 70s, with even mid-70 dew points in 
NW Iowa. Heat index values will continue to rise to 95 to 105 
degrees and current heat advisory will remain in place. 

Through the region a few clusters of elevated showers and 
thunderstorms continue. This activity is tied to both weak vorticity 
moving through the High Plains, but also west of a slightly richer 
850:700 mb theta-e airmass.  Latest guidance continues to suggest 
that cluster of activity just west of the CWA will continue to move 
north and northeast but could graze Beadle county later this 
afternoon. Activity over south central Nebraska is also expected to 
slowly crawl eastward, but without a strong theta-e push, may 
diminish by time it would reach Sioux City this evening. The 
development of any SFC based convection to the west and north seems 
limited given the strong EML in the area. If a storm could go, then 
large hail could be possible. 

TONIGHT:  There seems to be at least modest agreement in guidance 
tonight, suggesting continued mid-lvl theta-e advection will place a 
corridor of increased moisture west of I-29 and towards the James 
River valley after midnight.  Guidance also seems in agreement that 
another weak perturbation will leave Colorado and move northeast, 
inducing a 40 knot LLJ that will converge near the western half of 
the CWA.  Scattered showers and thunderstorm development would be 
favorable by 2-3am in this scenario. Environmental soundings 
would suggest anywhere from 1500-2000 J/KG MUCAPE lifted off the
700 mb layer, with modest shear AOA 25-30 knots. This would 
favor mostly multicells with some potential supercell 
characteristic, with brief bouts of quarter to ping pong ball 
hail. Feel perhaps the greatest risk given dry subcloud layer 
and steep low-lvl lapse rates would be some brief gusty winds. 
Storm motion may be very slow with mean winds only around 10 
knots, suggesting that with deep warm cloud depths and 
increasing PWATs, some localized heavy rain might be an issue. 
HREF/REFS 3hr PMM and max guidance indicates pockets of rainfall
of 2-4" could be possible. 

SATURDAY:  Lingering morning activity will continue to pose a few 
severe risks in the morning if any cold pool could develop. Though 
as the LLJ wanes and veers off, the convection risks may drop by 
early afternoon.  Lingering cloud debris, if storms develop, will 
pose a challenge to the afternoon forecast with some guidance 
keeping this festering cloud cover right through the heart of the 
CWA.  Currently forecast highs in the 90s are contingent on less 
cloud cover by mid-day.  If cloud cover doesn't impact us as much, 
then another advisory could be needed south of I-90 as dew points 
remain in the 70s.  Subsidence appears to remain in place for most 
of Saturday night, though the LLJ may once again spur isolated to 
scattered convection by daybreak Sunday. The various mesoscale waves 
topping the ridge into Sunday also pose an issue, with one or more 
convective clusters moving east and southeast out of North Dakota by 
daybreak. 

SUNDAY: Uncertainty grows on Sunday with the Tri-State are remaining 
under the synoptic ridge.  Convection on the periphery of this ridge 
will pose both a risk of dipping into the eastern CWA early Sunday, 
but moreso throwing a convective outflow boundary westward. If a 
boundary develops, it would certainly pose a risk for redevelopment 
later in the day despite a continued EML overhead. There remains far 
too much uncertainty in the forecast to be much more specific on 
severe weather risks, but those with outdoor plans should continue 
to monitor. Again, convection will have some impact on 
temperatures, but another day with highs in the upper 80s to 
lower 90s will be possible. 

MONDAY-TUESDAY: The apex of the mid-lvl ridge slides east of the Tri-
State by Monday as a deep upper trough moves into the Northern. 
Rockies. What will this pattern shift signal for us?  Lee-side 
troughing will induce stronger return flow into the Plains, 
with gusty surface winds by Monday afternoon. An approaching 
front late on Monday into Monday night could spur isolated to 
scattered thunderstorms over the Dakotas and Nebraska. Should 
boundary layer moisture not mix-out too significantly, a severe 
weather risk may develop into Tuesday night. Those limitations 
to any widespread risks may be the fact the deepest moisture 
transport is pushed north of the CWA along with the strongest 
forcing, suggesting lift along the boundary may be weaker 
further south. Temperatures will remain in the upper 80s, with 
the front moving southeast Tuesday. Again, we'll watch the 
positioning of this boundary for potential convection Tuesday 
afternoon. 

WEDNESDAY-THUR
